Small gotchas from building an analytics script

November 11, 2026•code

Building Puls I’ve hit a bunch of small bugs. None of them big enough for a post on their own. But together they’re a pretty good list of things I didn’t know, or knew and forgot.

So for my own sake, here they are.

document.currentScript is null for injected scripts

The tracking script reads its settings from data-* attributes on its own script tag. The easy way to find your own tag is document.currentScript.

Works great. Until someone injects the script with document.createElement('script'), like a tag manager or a consent tool does. Then currentScript is null.

The fix is a fallback that looks for the tag with querySelector, by its src and data-site attribute.

Reading innerWidth cost 116 ms

PageSpeed complained about a forced reflow on one of my sites, and pointed at Puls. About 116 ms of it.

The first beacon included the screen width, and it was sent right away on load. Reading innerWidth at that point forces the browser to calculate layout before it’s ready.

Wrapping the first beacon in requestIdleCallback (with a setTimeout fallback) fixed it. The browser settles the layout first, then Puls asks. Nobody needs their pageview logged in the first millisecond anyway.

Bots can break json_encode

One day a site’s dashboard was just empty. No error. Nothing.

Puls logs broken links, so 404s with their path. Scanner bots try path traversal with things like %C0%AE, which is invalid UTF-8. That got stored. And when the API tried to return it, json_encode failed and returned false. Silently.

json_encode($data, JSON_INVALID_UTF8_SUBSTITUTE);

That flag replaces invalid bytes instead of giving up. I also clean the path before storing it now, and /etc/passwd is on the list of paths that are just noise.

“Last 7 days” was 8 days

The comparison mode shows the previous period next to the current one, bar by bar. And the rightmost bar, today, never had anything to compare with.

days=7 meant “since 7 days ago”. That’s today plus 7 earlier days. Eight dates. The previous period was exactly seven. So when the bars were paired by index, today got paired with nothing.

Most visible on a one-day view, where half the bars had nothing to compare with. Now “last N days” is N dates including today.

Capture phase, and then not

Puls can track form submits automatically. The first version listened on body and missed a lot, because forms handled with JavaScript often call stopPropagation().

So I moved it to document in the capture phase. That catches the event before anyone can stop it.

But then it counted everything. Search boxes, forms that never actually submit, things handled by JavaScript with preventDefault(). Not really “submits”.

So it went back to the bubble phase, and skips the event if defaultPrevented is set. Sometimes the fix for the fix is going back, just a bit smarter.

One migration marker for all databases

Puls tracked which migrations had run with a .schema_version file in the data folder. One file. But you can have several databases in that folder, and locally I often did.

So one database was marked as migrated while the others still had the old schema.

SQLite has this built in, per database:

PRAGMA user_version;      -- read
PRAGMA user_version = 19; -- write

It’s just an integer in the database header that SQLite never uses for anything else. Perfect for a migration number.

That’s the list for now. I’m sure there will be more. All the fixes are in the Puls repo if you want to see the code.
